Asset Tracking Dashboards on ArcGIS Online

Sharper Shape GroupGeospatial Data EngineerInternal production tooling

An FME workspace that reconciles three separate systems into a single published ArcGIS Online feature service, so anyone running a utility inspection project can open a dashboard and see what has been captured against what has been delivered. Built once, then deployed and maintained across more than ten projects.

No client data is shown here. These dashboards track live inspection work for North American electric utilities, so circuit names, asset identifiers, project codes and network geometry all stay out of this page. The figure below is illustrative and the architecture is described rather than screenshotted. Happy to walk through it in conversation.

The problem

A helicopter inspection project flies the circuits of an electric utility and captures every pole structure along them. Two questions get asked constantly for the length of the project: what has been flown, and what has actually been handed to the client.

The answers lived in three different places. Capture state sat in the asset system, reachable only through its API. Delivery state sat on a Monday board, maintained by the delivery team. The circuits themselves were geometry in GIS. Answering something as ordinary as "how many span miles are still outstanding on this circuit" meant three people, an export from each system, and a spreadsheet to line them up. By the time the answer arrived it was already out of date.

What gets reconciled

Capture state
Pulled from the asset system over HTTP, then fragmented and flattened out of nested JSON into flat features. Each structure carries its asset identifier, whether it has been flown, and when.
Delivery state
Read from the delivery team's Monday board through a dedicated sub-workspace, giving each item its delivery status and the date it moved.
Circuit geometry
Joined spatially, so every structure inherits the circuit it belongs to rather than relying on a key that someone has to maintain by hand.
Measurement
Buffering, area and length calculation turn the joined result into the span miles and coverage areas the dashboard gauges actually read. Structures outside project scope are flagged and excluded rather than silently dropped.

Talking to Monday

Monday is the least pleasant part of the pipeline and the part I am most pleased with. Its API is not a straightforward REST resource: boards are addressed by id, columns come back as encoded values rather than named fields, and a single query returns a deeply nested structure that changes shape depending on what the board contains.

Four Python steps inside the workspace handle it. They resolve the boards, issue the queries, and parse the responses down into flat attributes that the rest of the workspace can treat like any other feature. Everything downstream of that point is ordinary FME, which is the point: the mess is contained in one place instead of spreading through the workspace.

Publishing, and why it scaled

The workspace writes directly to ArcGIS Online through a named connection, into its own folder, in batches of 200 features, reprojected to Web Mercator so the dashboard needs no conversion of its own.

The writer is configured to create the feature service if it is missing and to use the existing one if it is not. That single choice is what made this repeatable. The first run provisions the hosted layer, every run after updates it in place, and the dashboard built on top keeps pointing at the same service. Setting up a new project means re-pointing the workspace, not rebuilding the publishing step, which is how the same pipeline ended up serving more than ten projects.

Published to FME Flow so it runs on the server rather than a desktop, which also removes the person who used to be the one running it.

Outcome

  • Three disconnected systems reconciled into one authoritative layer per project
  • Captured against delivered readable at a glance instead of assembled by hand
  • Feature services that provision themselves on first run and update in place after
  • Deployed and maintained across more than ten inspection projects
  • The reporting step removed from the critical path of anyone's day
